Prevention: Potato scab is a soil-borne disease
Plant certified disease-free seed-tubers of tolerant varieties, e.g.
Arnova, Caruso, Derby, Faluka, Jelly, Manitou, Musica and
Disinfect infected seed tubers through heat-treatment (10 min in water at 55°C) before planting
Four years’ rotation of potatoes with maize, beans, onions or kales and
NOT tomato, eggplant, carrot or spinach to reduce the levels of soil-borne bacterium inoculum in potato field
If the disease is known from your area, then do not apply manure to potato fields, as it can increase scab infection

Irrigate to field capacity or to saturation, avoiding standing water during the 2 to 6 weeks following tuber formation
Monitoring: Potato scab is a bacterial disease that affects the tubers.
Optimum temperature for infection is 20-22°C, but disease can occur in soil within a range of 10-31°C.
Begin to search for infection symptoms usually at onset of tuberization
No clear symptoms can be seen on the stems or leaves.
Therefore, randomly select 4 plants from each 10th row of plants per acre at 6-8 weeks after planting, shovel away the soil a bit and remove 1-3 tubers per plant.
Then look for circular scab lesions or look for large scabby areas on the tuber
Look for corky, deeply pitted (rough surfaces) areas on the potato tubers, roughly circular, 5-10 mm diameter.
Direct Control: Isolate the diseased area by fencing-off (marking the affected area with string on boundary) to warn people not to enter and therefore not to spread the bacteria to non- infested field parts
Cover infected plant in a sack, uproot and bury (at least 50 cm deep) outside the field immediately.
Be careful not the spread the disease
Restrictions: There is no chemical control option available against this disease
